# Order-to-Delivery: Diagnostic Charter and Mobilisation Request

**Version 2.0 — Not a request to approve a solution. A request to approve a six-week, jointly-staffed diagnostic with a defined decision gate.**

Prepared for the Operations Steering Group. To be circulated for comment to the Plant Manager, the Quality Manager, and the three Sales regional heads **before** it is tabled, so that any concern arrives as a revision to this draft rather than as a disagreement in the room. Not for customer-facing use. No change to the published lead-time schedule is sought or implied by this paper.

---

## How this differs from Version 1.0

Version 1.0 asked for a decision on a hypothesis. That was our error, and the criticism was fair. This version separates what we believe from what we know, places the analysis of the previous failure **first** rather than last, and asks the Steering Group for one narrow, reversible thing: permission to measure, with a named senior owner and a joint team. Every quantified figure below is labelled **[Established]**, **[Estimate — source stated]**, or **[Hypothesis — test stated]**. Where a number is a hypothesis, we have written down what result would prove us wrong.

---

## 1. What we are asking for on this page

| Item | Request |
|---|---|
| **Decision sought now** | Approve a **6-week diagnostic** (Workstreams A–E, §3–§7), a **single accountable owner** (§9.1), and a **joint three-function team** (§9.5). Estimated cost: 0.7 FTE-months of internal time plus ~$40k external testing/teardown support **[Estimate — based on prior VSM exercises]** |
| **Decision explicitly NOT sought now** | Any inventory build. Any change to inspection routings. Any change to quoted lead times. Any customer communication. Any capital release |
| **First real decision point** | **Gate 1, week 6.** The diagnostic returns with a falsifiable finding and a costed options paper. The Steering Group may then approve, redirect, or stop |
| **Our working hypothesis (to be tested, not assumed)** | The 14-week span is dominated by waiting, supplier lead time and approval loops rather than by work content or by the certified inspections themselves. If so, the answer is a **segmented promise** supported by a **semi-finished decoupling bank**, **inspection capacity added rather than gates removed**, and **variability reduction** — not compression of the existing single process |
| **The condition that would falsify it** | If hands-on work content exceeds **40% of quoted span**, or if certified inspection *execution* (not queue) exceeds **15%**, segmentation and inventory are the wrong answers and we pivot to capacity addition and variability reduction. We will report this outcome as readily as the other |
| **Non-negotiable, from the outset** | **No certified inspection is removed, resequenced or sampled during this programme without the Quality Manager's written agreement, which is not appealable to the Steering Group or to the Managing Director.** §6.1 |

We would rather return at week 6 having disproved our own hypothesis than proceed on it now. Given the history described in §2, we think the organisation will accept a slow start far more readily than a second confident start.

---

## 2. First, the last attempt — the most valuable dataset we own

The previous compression attempt produced a warranty spike that took two years to recover from. Version 1.0 treated this as a feeling to be respected. That was a mistake of judgement. It is evidence, and it must be analysed before anything else is proposed. Nothing else in this paper will earn Quality's or Production's cooperation if this is skipped.

**Workstream A — Defect-escape reconstruction. Owner: Quality Manager. Duration: weeks 1–4. Deliverable: a defect-escape map.**

| Step | Method | Output |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | Extract all warranty claims for units shipped in the compression window and the 18 months following | Claim population, cost, and 12-month PPM by shipment cohort |
| A2 | Pareto by **failure mode**, not by product or by customer | Which 3–5 modes carried the cost |
| A3 | For each mode, trace to the specific process change that permitted the escape — reduced inspection frequency, overlapped operations, expedited supplier substitution, overtime hours, retrospective paperwork, unapproved deviation authority | A causal map: change → escape → cost |
| A4 | For each cause, state the specific control now in place, or absent | The list Quality will hold this programme against |

**The candidate causes we intend to test** (stated so the team can disprove them, not so the answer is pre-written): inspection frequency reduced from 100% to sampling without a capability study; welding and NDT overlapped so that rework occurred after downstream assembly; substitute material or supplier accepted on expedite without full first-article approval; sustained overtime raising defect generation at the same time inspection was reduced; documentation completed after the fact, removing the gate's real function while leaving its record intact.

**Why this comes first:** the sceptics in the building are not asking to be reassured. They are asking one question — *what exactly did we break, and what specifically prevents us breaking it again?* Section A4 is the only honest answer. If A1–A4 shows that the escapes came from removing internal checks, then a large part of what Version 1.0 proposed is simply prohibited, and we will say so in the Gate 1 paper.

**Correction to Version 1.0.** Version 1.0 proposed removing "internally-accreted inspections that no code requires." That is very close to the class of action that plausibly caused the last failure, and we withdraw the phrasing. See §6.1 for the replacement rule.

---

## 3. Second, is the problem the problem? — validating the commercial premise

Sales reports losing one deal in three on delivery speed alone. We do not doubt the report, and we want to be careful about how the following is read: the purpose is not to test Sales' honesty. It is to protect Sales from being handed a solution that does not win the deals they are actually losing. Lost-reason coding is the weakest data in any commercial system in any company, ours included, because "we lost on lead time" is the answer that costs no one anything, whereas "we lost on price" and "we lost on specification" both cost someone something.

**Workstream B — Loss anatomy. Owner: Commercial Director, with an interviewer from outside Sales (Finance or the programme office). Weeks 1–5.**

| B1 | Re-code the last 24 months of losses from CRM narrative, quotes and correspondence — not from the summary field |
| B2 | **Segment losses by product class** (pre-configured / bounded-option / engineered-to-order) and by competitor |
| B3 | 15–20 structured win/loss interviews, conducted by the non-Sales interviewer, buyer-side |
| B4 | Price-realisation analysis on *won* deals: are we winning on discount where we quote long? |
| B5 | Quoted-vs-actual delivery on our own won orders: how often do we hit 14 weeks? |

**The finding that would change the whole plan.** If the lost deals are concentrated in engineered-to-order work, then a plan that shortens the standard platforms and leaves ETO at 14 weeks addresses none of the stated problem while consuming the entire budget. This is a live possibility — ETO is precisely where a competitor's standard offering cannot play and where buyers press hardest on schedule. **We will segment the lost pipeline before we segment the promise**, and B2 is the gating output for §5.

**Workstream C — Competitor teardown. Owner: Product Management with Engineering. Weeks 2–6.** The six-week competitor quote is the single load-bearing assumption behind any inventory investment, and we currently have no evidence about it. Questions: which configurations do they actually quote at six weeks, and which do they quietly quote longer? Do they *deliver* at six, or quote six and slip? Is their scope narrower — fewer options, lighter certification, a different code class? Are they holding finished or semi-finished modules, and who funds that? Are they buying schedule with price or with penalty exposure? Evidence: purchased-unit teardown, ex-employee and shared-distributor input, published terms, and two buy-side interviews from B3.

If they quote six weeks on genuinely comparable engineered scope, the decoupling-bank thesis collapses and we will report that at Gate 1.

---

## 4. Third, where the time actually goes — with definitions

Version 1.0 asserted "79% of the critical path is waiting." The figure was undefined and therefore not checkable, in a document that asked to be checked. Definitions first.

- **Quoted span** = calendar span from order acceptance to ex-works readiness = 14 weeks = **70 working days** **[Established — from the published schedule]**
- **Touch time** = hands-on work on the product, *including the execution of certified inspections*. It excludes all queue, all approval waiting, all movement, all supplier span
- **Non-touch span** = the remainder, disaggregated below by *who controls it*, which is the only breakdown that matters for action

**Hypothesised decomposition of a representative Class-A-equivalent order** **[Hypothesis — to be replaced by measured data in Workstream D]**:

| Block | Days | Controlled by | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Order entry, application engineering, drawing release | 8 | Us | Non-touch |
| **Customer** approval of drawings, credit clearance, spec churn after order entry | 5 | **Customer** | Non-touch |
| Long-lead purchased items (governing item only) | 20 | Supplier | Non-touch |
| Fabrication and machining | 9 | Us | **Touch** |
| Queue and movement between fabrication operations | 12 | Us | Non-touch |
| Certified inspection execution (all gates) | 3 | Us | **Touch** |
| **Waiting for an inspector, and for sign-off/paperwork after inspection** | 8 | Us | Non-touch |
| Final assembly and functional test | 3 | Us | **Touch** |
| Documentation pack, preservation, freight staging | 2 | Us | Non-touch |
| **Total** | **70** | | **Touch 15 (21%) / Non-touch 55 (79%)** |

Read correctly, the 79% is not one problem but four, of very different kinds: **20 days supplier span**, **13 days front end of which 5 are the customer's**, **20 days internal queue and movement**, **2 days closing administration**. Only the 20 days of internal queue is available to conventional flow improvement. That is why Version 1.0's implied "attack waiting" was too glib.

**The most important line in the table is the 8 days waiting for an inspector against 3 days of inspection.** If measurement confirms it, then the certified gates are not the constraint — *inspection capacity and its variability* is. That reframes the entire quality argument: the lever is **more inspection availability, not less inspection**.

**Workstream D — Joint time study. Owner: programme owner. Team: one Production, one Quality, one Sales/order-management representative, working the same 20 orders together. Weeks 1–6.** Method: 20 recently completed orders traced date-stamp by date-stamp, plus 5 live orders shadowed. Every day of the 70 is assigned to a block and to a controller. Customer-caused delay is recorded separately and never netted into internal performance — otherwise we would promise six weeks and lose it inside an approval loop we do not control.

The team composition here is deliberate. The three functions each hold a partial and internally consistent account of the delay, and each is correct about the others in part. Our experience is that a dispute of this kind is not settled by a paper. It is settled when the three people who disagree collect the same numbers side by side, and none of them has to say in a meeting that they were wrong.

---

## 5. Fourth, capacity and variability — before any inventory or sequencing proposal

**Workstream E — Load and variability. Owner: Plant Manager with Finance. Weeks 2–6.**

Queue time is not linear in loading. Above roughly 85% utilisation of a constraint resource it rises steeply, and rises again with arrival and process variability. The practical consequence is uncomfortable and must be stated before we propose anything: **if the plant and the inspection function are loaded above ~85%, a 16-day inventory saving will be quietly reabsorbed as queue within two quarters, and we will have spent working capital to buy nothing.** That is a plausible reading of what happened in part last time — the schedule was compressed while the load was unchanged, so the only remaining source of speed was the gates.

Required outputs before any Gate 1 recommendation:

1. Load vs. capacity by constraint resource, monthly, 12 months back and 6 forward — **including certified inspectors as a resource**, with holiday, training and certification-renewal absence modelled
2. Arrival variability at each certified gate (coefficient of variation of arrivals and of inspection duration)
3. Order-release discipline: how much WIP is on the floor against what a CONWIP cap would allow
4. Rework loops as a variability source — first-pass yield by operation, and how much of the 12-day inter-operation queue is actually rework waiting
5. Options and costs for: one additional certified inspector; cross-certifying two existing production engineers to inspect (with the independence question addressed explicitly); moving inspection to the work rather than the work to inspection; levelled order release

---

## 6. How the quality gates are protected — stated as rules, not as intentions

These four rules are proposed as standing policy for the programme, to be recorded in the minute and countersigned by the Quality Manager. They apply from the day the diagnostic starts, not from Gate 1.

**6.1 The removal test — the burden of proof sits on removal.**
No inspection is removed, reduced in frequency, or moved to sampling on the grounds that no code requires it. *Not code-required* is not *not value-adding*; several of our internal checks almost certainly exist because a customer was harmed once and the reason was never written down. An inspection may be proposed for change **only** where at least **12 months of defect-find data** show that it has found no defect that a defined downstream gate would not also have found, **and** the Quality Manager agrees in writing. **That agreement is not appealable — not to this Steering Group, and not to the Managing Director.** Where records are insufficient to run the test, the answer is no, and the inspection stays.

**6.2 Queue reduction is unlimited; gate reduction is near-prohibited.** Time spent *waiting for* an inspection is programme territory. Time spent *performing* one is not. Our expectation is that all quality-related time savings come from the 8 days of waiting and sign-off, and none from the 3 days of inspection.

**6.3 Certification integrity of any inventory bank must be established before, not after, any build.** Holding semi-finished certified modules raises questions we do not yet know the answers to, and they must be closed by the certifying body in writing at Gate 1, not discovered at Gate 2: does inspection status survive storage, and for how long? How are material certificates and heat traceability re-linked at configuration? Are there preservation, shelf-life or re-test requirements? **Does the notified body have to approve the revised inspection sequence, and how long does that approval itself take?** An unnoticed re-qualification requirement could add months and would change the whole business case. Add to the risk register at the highest severity.

**6.4 Published halt tripwires, agreed before we start, triggered by Quality alone.** Any one of the following halts the programme and reverts affected orders to the current routing, without a meeting and without discussion:

| Tripwire | Threshold |
|---|---|
| First-pass yield at any certified gate | Falls below the trailing 12-mont…[truncated]

# Global Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative
## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). It answers the questions the first draft deferred — most importantly what the centre itself is bound by (§9). And the regional material has been re-cut so that no colleague opens it and finds their country described inside someone else's card.

The regional cards in §6 remain what they were: **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where a region has its own diagnostic data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired for that unit (§5.4). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies we would ask the sponsor group to extend before this travels further. First, that the fourteen regional people leads and the four regional MDs see §§3, 4 and 9 and have time to respond in their own way before the board pack is assembled — a programme about devolved authority that arrives in a region fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §10 (consultation and legal gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward before any part of this is described to employees anywhere. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the gap likely sits · behaviour to add · behaviour to drop · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 60** · legal or structural watch item.

### 5.3 The 60-day indicator, and why it is on every card
The failure modes that matter most — courteous non-adoption, affirmative response with no movement — are precisely the ones you cannot detect by asking. Each card therefore names an observable proxy visible within 60 days.

### 5.4 The supersession rule
**Where unit-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that unit.** Within-country variance in work values routinely exceeds between-country variance; function, site history and acquisition lineage frequently dominate nationality. This applies to every card, not only where we have noted it.

### 5.5 Scope note
Cards cover the fourteen clusters where we have wholly-owned or majority-controlled operations. Russia and Belarus are **out of scope** for this programme pending the Group's standing position on those entities; the programme director should not open a workstream there without a written instruction from the sponsor group.

---

## 6. Regional cards

### Card A — Anglosphere (US, Canada, UK, Ireland, Australia, New Zealand)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low authority distance; direct disagreement acceptable; individual error attribution; moderate-to-high ambiguity tolerance |
| Likely gap | Not permission — **follow-through**. Voice is already loud; evidence that it changes anything is thin |
| Add | Visible closure loops: "here is what we did with what you told us, here is what we declined, and why" |
| Drop | Announcing empowerment. The region has heard it and discounts it |
| Failure mode | Ironic compliance; strong survey movement, unchanged decision latency |
| 60-day indicator | Ratio of raised items with a documented, dated response — target 80%+; skip-level uptake |
| Watch item | Strong individual error attribution and litigation exposure make Entitlement III hard: blame follows the name. US at-will/discipline documentation practice cuts against visible error absorption |
| Internal variance not to flatten | UK indirectness is closer to the Nordic-plus-hedging pattern than to US directness; Quebec sits closer to Card C than to the rest of Canada; the Australian register tolerates challenge to authority that would be career-limiting in the US |

### Card B — Germanic & Nordic (DE, AT, CH, NL, SE, DK, NO, FI)

| | |
|---|---|
| Working hypothesis | Low-to-moderate authority distance, expertise-derived; very direct disagreement; system-oriented error attribution; **low ambiguity tolerance** |

**Workstream A — Defect-escape reconstruction. Owner: Quality Manager. Duration: weeks 1–4. Deliverable: a defect-escape map.**

| Step | Method | Output |
|---|---|---|
| A1 | Extract all warranty claims for units shipped in the compression window and the 18 months following | Claim population, cost, and 12-month PPM by shipment cohort |
| A2 | Pareto by **failure mode**, not by product or by customer | Which 3–5 modes carried the cost |
| A3 | For each mode, trace to the specific process change that permitted the escape — reduced inspection frequency, overlapped operations, expedited supplier substitution, overtime hours, retrospective paperwork, unapproved deviation authority | A causal map: change → escape → cost |
| A4 | For each cause, state the specific control now in place, or absent | The list Quality will hold this programme against |

**The candidate causes we intend to test** (stated so the team can disprove them, not so the answer is pre-written): inspection frequency reduced from 100% to sampling without a capability study; welding and NDT overlapped so that rework occurred after downstream assembly; substitute material or supplier accepted on expedite without full first-article approval; sustained overtime raising defect generation at the same time inspection was reduced; documentation completed after the fact, removing the gate's real function while leaving its record intact.

**Why this comes first:** the sceptics in the building are not asking to be reassured. They are asking one question — *what exactly did we break, and what specifically prevents us breaking it again?* Section A4 is the only honest answer. If A1–A4 shows that the escapes came from removing internal checks, then a large part of what Version 1.0 proposed is simply prohibited, and we will say so in the Gate 1 paper.

**Correction to Version 1.0.** Version 1.0 proposed removing "internally-accreted inspections that no code requires." That is very close to the class of action that plausibly caused the last failure, and we withdraw the phrasing. See §6.1 for the replacement rule.

---

## 3. Second, is the problem the problem? — validating the commercial premise

Sales reports losing one deal in three on delivery speed alone. We do not doubt the report, and we want to be careful about how the following is read: the purpose is not to test Sales' honesty. It is to protect Sales from being handed a solution that does not win the deals they are actually losing. Lost-reason coding is the weakest data in any commercial system in any company, ours included, because "we lost on lead time" is the answer that costs no one anything, whereas "we lost on price" and "we lost on specification" both cost someone something.

**Workstream B — Loss anatomy. Owner: Commercial Director, with an interviewer from outside Sales (Finance or the programme office). Weeks 1–5.**

| B1 | Re-code the last 24 months of losses from CRM narrative, quotes and correspondence — not from the summary field |
| B2 | **Segment losses by product class** (pre-configured / bounded-option / engineered-to-order) and by competitor |
| B3 | 15–20 structured win/loss interviews, conducted by the non-Sales interviewer, buyer-side |
| B4 | Price-realisation analysis on *won* deals: are we winning on discount where we quote long? |
| B5 | Quoted-vs-actual delivery on our own won orders: how often do we hit 14 weeks? |

**The finding that would change the whole plan.** If the lost deals are concentrated in engineered-to-order work, then a plan that shortens the standard platforms and leaves ETO at 14 weeks addresses none of the stated problem while consuming the entire budget. This is a live possibility — ETO is precisely where a competitor's standard offering cannot play and where buyers press hardest on schedule. **We will segment the lost pipeline before we segment the promise**, and B2 is the gating output for §5.

**Workstream C — Competitor teardown. Owner: Product Management with Engineering. Weeks 2–6.** The six-week competitor quote is the single load-bearing assumption behind any inventory investment, and we currently have no evidence about it. Questions: which configurations do they actually quote at six weeks, and which do they quietly quote longer? Do they *deliver* at six, or quote six and slip? Is their scope narrower — fewer options, lighter certification, a different code class? Are they holding finished or semi-finished modules, and who funds that? Are they buying schedule with price or with penalty exposure? Evidence: purchased-unit teardown, ex-employee and shared-distributor input, published terms, and two buy-side interviews from B3.

If they quote six weeks on genuinely comparable engineered scope, the decoupling-bank thesis collapses and we will report that at Gate 1.

---

## 4. Third, where the time actually goes — with definitions

Version 1.0 asserted "79% of the critical path is waiting." The figure was undefined and therefore not checkable, in a document that asked to be checked. Definitions first.

- **Quoted span** = calendar span from order acceptance to ex-works readiness = 14 weeks = **70 working days** **[Established — from the published schedule]**
- **Touch time** = hands-on work on the product, *including the execution of certified inspections*. It excludes all queue, all approval waiting, all movement, all supplier span
- **Non-touch span** = the remainder, disaggregated below by *who controls it*, which is the only breakdown that matters for action

**Hypothesised decomposition of a representative Class-A-equivalent order** **[Hypothesis — to be replaced by measured data in Workstream D]**:

| Block | Days | Controlled by | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| Order entry, application engineering, drawing release | 8 | Us | Non-touch |
| **Customer** approval of drawings, credit clearance, spec churn after order entry | 5 | **Customer** | Non-touch |
| Long-lead purchased items (governing item only) | 20 | Supplier | Non-touch |
| Fabrication and machining | 9 | Us | **Touch** |
| Queue and movement between fabrication operations | 12 | Us | Non-touch |
| Certified inspection execution (all gates) | 3 | Us | **Touch** |
| **Waiting for an inspector, and for sign-off/paperwork after inspection** | 8 | Us | Non-touch |
| Final assembly and functional test | 3 | Us | **Touch** |
| Documentation pack, preservation, freight staging | 2 | Us | Non-touch |
| **Total** | **70** | | **Touch 15 (21%) / Non-touch 55 (79%)** |

Read correctly, the 79% is not one problem but four, of very different kinds: **20 days supplier span**, **13 days front end of which 5 are the customer's**, **20 days internal queue and movement**, **2 days closing administration**. Only the 20 days of internal queue is available to conventional flow improvement. That is why Version 1.0's implied "attack waiting" was too glib.

**The most important line in the table is the 8 days waiting for an inspector against 3 days of inspection.** If measurement confirms it, then the certified gates are not the constraint — *inspection capacity and its variability* is. That reframes the entire quality argument: the lever is **more inspection availability, not less inspection**.

**Workstream D — Joint time study. Owner: programme owner. Team: one Production, one Quality, one Sales/order-management representative, working the same 20 orders together. Weeks 1–6.** Method: 20 recently completed orders traced date-stamp by date-stamp, plus 5 live orders shadowed. Every day of the 70 is assigned to a block and to a controller. Customer-caused delay is recorded separately and never netted into internal performance — otherwise we would promise six weeks and lose it inside an approval loop we do not control.

The team composition here is deliberate. The three functions each hold a partial and internally consistent account of the delay, and each is correct about the others in part. Our experience is that a dispute of this kind is not settled by a paper. It is settled when the three people who disagree collect the same numbers side by side, and none of them has to say in a meeting that they were wrong.

---

## 5. Fourth, capacity and variability — before any inventory or sequencing proposal

**Workstream E — Load and variability. Owner: Plant Manager with Finance. Weeks 2–6.**

Queue time is not linear in loading. Above roughly 85% utilisation of a constraint resource it rises steeply, and rises again with arrival and process variability. The practical consequence is uncomfortable and must be stated before we propose anything: **if the plant and the inspection function are loaded above ~85%, a 16-day inventory saving will be quietly reabsorbed as queue within two quarters, and we will have spent working capital to buy nothing.** That is a plausible reading of what happened in part last time — the schedule was compressed while the load was unchanged, so the only remaining source of speed was the gates.

Required outputs before any Gate 1 recommendation:

1. Load vs. capacity by constraint resource, monthly, 12 months back and 6 forward — **including certified inspectors as a resource**, with holiday, training and certification-renewal absence modelled
2. Arrival variability at each certified gate (coefficient of variation of arrivals and of inspection duration)
3. Order-release discipline: how much WIP is on the floor against what a CONWIP cap would allow
4. Rework loops as a variability source — first-pass yield by operation, and how much of the 12-day inter-operation queue is actually rework waiting
5. Options and costs for: one additional certified inspector; cross-certifying two existing production engineers to inspect (with the independence question addressed explicitly); moving inspection to the work rather than the work to inspection; levelled order release

---

## 6. How the quality gates are protected — stated as rules, not as intentions

These four rules are proposed as standing policy for the programme, to be recorded in the minute and countersigned by the Quality Manager. They apply from the day the diagnostic starts, not from Gate 1.

**6.1 The removal test — the burden of proof sits on removal.**
No inspection is removed, reduced in frequency, or moved to sampling on the grounds that no code requires it. *Not code-required* is not *not value-adding*; several of our internal checks almost certainly exist because a customer was harmed once and the reason was never written down. An inspection may be proposed for change **only** where at least **12 months of defect-find data** show that it has found no defect that a defined downstream gate would not also have found, **and** the Quality Manager agrees in writing. **That agreement is not appealable — not to this Steering Group, and not to the Managing Director.** Where records are insufficient to run the test, the answer is no, and the inspection stays.

**6.2 Queue reduction is unlimited; gate reduction is near-prohibited.** Time spent *waiting for* an inspection is programme territory. Time spent *performing* one is not. Our expectation is that all quality-related time savings come from the 8 days of waiting and sign-off, and none from the 3 days of inspection.

**6.3 Certification integrity of any inventory bank must be established before, not after, any build.** Holding semi-finished certified modules raises questions we do not yet know the answers to, and they must be closed by the certifying body in writing at Gate 1, not discovered at Gate 2: does inspection status survive storage, and for how long? How are material certificates and heat traceability re-linked at configuration? Are there preservation, shelf-life or re-test requirements? **Does the notified body have to approve the revised inspection sequence, and how long does that approval itself take?** An unnoticed re-qualification requirement could add months and would change the whole business case. Add to the risk register at the highest severity.

**6.4 Published halt tripwires, agreed before we start, triggered by Quality alone.** Any one of the following halts the programme and reverts affected orders to the current routing, without a meeting and without discussion:

| Tripwire | Threshold |
|---|---|
| First-pass yield at any certified gate | Falls below the trailing 12-month baseline by more than 2 points over any 10 consecutive units |
| Escapes found at final inspection | Any increase over baseline |
| Concessions / deviations raised | Any increase in rate |
| Supplier PPM on decoupled items | Above the agreed cap |
| Warranty claims, 12-month cohort | Any adverse trend against the pre-programme cohort |

Publishing these before the programme begins, with the trigger in Quality's hand alone, is the strongest signal we can offer to the colleagues who lived through the last attempt. It also means no one has to argue their case under pressure in a room where the schedule is the loudest voice.

---

## 7. The change portfolio we expect to recommend at Gate 1 — subject to Workstreams A–E

Presented as candidates with their evidential dependencies, so the Steering Group can see what each one is waiting on.

| Change | Mechanism | Depends on | Expected span effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Segmented promise** | Class A pre-configured platforms; Class B bounded options; Class C engineered-to-order | **B2 must show losses are not concentrated in Class C** | See §8 |
| **Semi-finished decoupling bank** | Base modules held two operations downstream of raw material | C (competitor evidence), E (loading), 6.3 (certification) | Removes ~20 supplier days + ~4 early-queue days, adds ~2–3 configuration/verification days for Class A. **Net 16–22 days [Hypothesis]** |
| **Supplier programme** (not one clause — a workstream) | Pareto of long-lead items; dual-source wherever a single-source lead time governs the critical path; VMI/consignment with **funding explicitly negotiated, our preference supplier-funded against a volume commitment**; capacity reservation agreements; **supplier PPM entry gate — no supplier joins the decoupled set without 12 months of PPM evidence**, since incoming supplier quality is a common and under-examined cause of warranty spikes | Workstream D governing-item analysis | Up to 20 days on the governing item |
